client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next month, and honestly, just thinking about them makes my chest tight. Last semester I did pretty badly in chemistry, and now I can't stop worrying that I'm going to fail again no matter how hard I study. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem feels so real and practical, you know?
therapist: It makes complete sense that your body is already reacting with that chest tightness — you're carrying a real weight, and last semester's experience has made this feel even more loaded and scary. I also hear your skepticism about whether talking helps, and that's actually a really honest and important thing to name; what we can do together is look closely at some of the thoughts driving that worry, because sometimes our mind treats a *fear* of failing as if it's already a *fact*. What does that inner voice actually tell you when you imagine sitting down to study — what's the specific thought that shows up most?

client: When I sit down to study, the first thing that pops into my head is something like, "What's the point, you're going to blank out on the test just like last time." It's almost like my brain is already writing the ending before I've even started, and then I just feel this wave of exhaustion on top of the anxiety. I guess I can see what you mean about fear versus fact, but it's hard to separate them when the fear feels so backed up by actual evidence from last semester.
therapist: That thought — "what's the point, you're going to blank out" — is such a heavy thing to carry before you've even opened a book, and it makes complete sense that exhaustion follows right behind it. You're right that last semester feels like evidence, but I want to gently explore that with you: did *everything* go wrong last semester, or did your brain selectively hold onto the hardest moments as the whole story? What do you actually remember about how you prepared and what happened — is there any part of last semester that didn't fit the "I always fail" narrative?

client: Okay, I mean... I did pass my other classes last semester, and I actually did alright in my history essay, which surprised me. But chemistry felt so different, so much harder, and that's the class I have again this semester, so it's not like those other wins really cancel out the specific thing I'm scared of. I hear what you're saying about selective memory, but I'm not sure pointing out that I passed history is going to make me feel less terrified when I'm staring at a chemistry equation.
therapist: You're making a really sharp and fair point — passing history doesn't magically dissolve the fear of chemistry, and I don't want to brush past that specific dread. But what you just did is actually significant: you pushed back on your own brain's story a little, noticing that "I always fail" isn't quite accurate, even if chemistry is its own real challenge. So I'm curious — when you think about what made chemistry harder last semester, do you have a sense of whether it was the material itself, how you studied, the circumstances, or something else entirely?

client: Honestly, looking back, I think a big part of it was that I kept putting off studying because every time I opened the textbook I felt so overwhelmed that I'd just shut it again. And then I'd feel guilty about not studying, which made me avoid it even more, so by the time the exam came I really hadn't prepared enough. So I guess it wasn't that I'm just fundamentally bad at chemistry, but I don't know how to break that cycle when the overwhelm hits just as hard this time around.
therapist: That's a really meaningful insight — you just identified that it wasn't a lack of ability that drove last semester's result, but a very understandable cycle of overwhelm leading to avoidance leading to guilt, and that cycle fed itself. The good news is that cycles have entry points, and what you've just described gives us something concrete to work with rather than a fixed story about who you are at chemistry. What do you think would happen if, instead of opening the whole textbook, you gave yourself permission to study for just five or ten minutes — small enough that the overwhelm doesn't get the first move?

client: I've actually heard the "just five minutes" thing before and honestly my first reaction is a little skeptical, because five minutes feels almost too small to matter when I have so much ground to cover. Like, I worry I'll do my five minutes and then feel like I've barely scratched the surface, and that'll just remind me how far behind I am. But I guess the guilt and avoidance cycle you described is real, so maybe the point isn't to cover everything in those five minutes, it's more about not letting the overwhelm win before I even start?
therapist: You just answered your own skepticism in a really insightful way — the point of those five minutes isn't to cover ground, it's to prove to your nervous system that opening the book doesn't have to trigger a crisis. That small act starts to quietly rewrite the story your brain has been telling, where chemistry equals overwhelm equals shutdown. What do you think it would feel like *after* those five minutes, if you closed the book having stayed with it instead of fleeing — even if you'd only read one page?

client: Honestly, I think I might feel a tiny bit relieved, like I'd proven something small to myself, but I'm also worried that feeling would be really short-lived before my brain jumps straight to "okay but you still have chapters four through twelve to go." I guess there's a part of me that doesn't fully trust that a small win would stick, because my anxiety has a way of just moving the goalposts the second I accomplish something. But maybe that's worth testing, even if I'm not totally convinced it'll work.
therapist: You've just named something really important — the "moving goalposts" pattern is actually a very common anxiety trick, where it robs you of credit the moment you earn it, so the win never quite lands. What we can work on is building in a deliberate moment of acknowledgment *before* your brain shifts to chapter four through twelve, almost like intercepting the goalpost-move before it happens. And I love that you ended with "maybe that's worth testing" — that's not full conviction, but it's enough to start; what would it look like for you to actually try this in the next day or two, and how might you remind yourself to pause and notice that small relief before anxiety rushes in to minimize it?

client: I think I could try it tomorrow evening, maybe just opening my chemistry notes for a few minutes after dinner when I'm not already exhausted. But the part about pausing to acknowledge the small relief feels a bit awkward to me, like I'm not sure what that actually looks like in practice — do I just sit there and tell myself "good job" out loud, because that honestly sounds a little forced? I guess I could try writing it down or something, but I'm worried even that will feel hollow if my anxiety is already loud in the background.
therapist: It's really good that you have a concrete plan for tomorrow evening — that's already more than just an idea. The acknowledgment doesn't have to feel like a pep talk; it can be as simple as writing one factual sentence, like "I opened my notes and stayed for five minutes," because the power isn't in the enthusiasm but in your brain registering that it actually happened. What do you think feels more natural to you — a quick written note, even just on your phone, or maybe just pausing for a breath and noticing the relief before closing the notes?

client: Writing one factual sentence on my phone actually sounds more doable than I expected, because it feels less like performing positivity and more like just recording what happened. I think I could manage that without it feeling too forced, though I'm a little worried that on a bad anxiety night I'll just skip it and tell myself it doesn't matter. I guess that's something I can't fully predict, but I'm willing to try it tomorrow and see how it actually feels in the moment.
therapist: You've moved from real skepticism at the start of our conversation to "I'm willing to try" — that's a genuinely meaningful shift, and it happened because you did the thinking, not because I convinced you. Your worry about skipping it on a hard night is fair, so it might help to decide *now* that skipping it doesn't mean the experiment failed — it just means that night was hard, and the next attempt still counts. How does it feel to give yourself that kind of permission in advance, where one missed entry doesn't erase the whole effort?

client: Honestly, that framing is a bit of a relief, because usually in my head it's all or nothing — either I follow through perfectly or I've already failed the whole thing. I think giving myself permission in advance feels strange but also kind of necessary, because I know my anxiety will try to use one missed night as proof that I'm hopeless. I'm not fully convinced I'll actually believe that permission when I'm in the middle of a bad night, but it's at least something I can try to hold onto.
therapist: You've just named one of the most central patterns in anxiety — that all-or-nothing thinking that turns a single missed night into evidence of total hopelessness, and simply seeing it clearly like that is already a small act of resistance against it. It makes complete sense that the permission feels strange, because your brain has been running on a harsher rulebook for a long time, and new rules take practice to actually feel true rather than just sound reasonable. As you head into tomorrow evening, what would you want to gently remind yourself if that all-or-nothing voice does show up — is there a short, honest phrase that feels like *yours*, not forced, that you could keep close?

client: I've been sitting with that question and the phrase that actually feels honest to me is something like "one step still counts," because it doesn't feel like I'm lying to myself or pretending everything is fine. It's simple enough that I might actually remember it when my brain is loud, though I'm a little skeptical I'll have the presence of mind to reach for it in the moment. I guess that's part of what I'd have to practice too, actually using it instead of just knowing it exists.
therapist: "One step still counts" is genuinely yours — it's honest, it's not performative, and that's exactly why it has a better chance of landing when things get loud. You're right that knowing a phrase and actually reaching for it in a hard moment are two different skills, and the only way to build that second one is through the kind of low-stakes practice you're already planning for tomorrow evening. What do you think it would feel like to look back on this conversation a week from now, having tried even imperfectly — what would feel different?
